To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hedonic price regression approach can be used to estimate marginal willingness to pay (WTP) for a reduction in pollution and that WTP is much higher when time-varying pollution levels are controlled for than when they are not controlled for.
ignoring time-varying, correlated unobservables in hedonic price regressions leads to an understatement of the benefits of a policy that reduces air pollution.

(i) we propose a new strategy to estimate hedonic price regressions in the presence of unobservable time-varying house or neighborhood characteristics, and (ii) our results suggest that ignoring this problem can lead to a significant understatement of the benefits from a pollution-reduction program.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of identifying the causal impact of a treatment, in this case a change in air pollution, on a particular outcome, the price of a house in the area affected.
a problem in hedonic price regressions that is both theoretically and practically important.

a pervasive problem in hedonic price regressions: how to control for time- varying correlated unobservables, and in particular, for the effects of time-vary- ing unobserved attributes of the product being sold.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hedonic price method is an effective and efficient way of valuing environmental quality.
the results of this study are consistent with the hypothesis that there is a positive relationship between the level of pollution and the price of the house.
the results of this paper show that ignoring bias from unobserved time-varying attributes of the house and neighborhood leads to an understatement of the benefits of reducing air pollution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hedonics is an extremely useful tool for estimating the value of environmental amenities.
hedonic pricing is not only a useful tool to estimate marginal willingness to pay but also a powerful tool for policy analysis.
the EPA's estimates of marginal willingness to pay are likely too low, but not by as much as the EPA's own estimates suggest.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of prior sales prices as controls can provide a powerful solution to a common problem in hedonic studies.
a theory-based approach can help address a common problem in hedonic price studies.
the standard hedonic price regression is a useful and practical tool for policy analysis, even when the unobservables problem is severe.
